name: Kusaal
confidence_why: Eddyshaw's 2026 reference grammar of Agolle Kusaal gives an explicit analysis of root stress (every root carries underlying stress, prefixes and most light monosyllables are unstressed), and the only dissent is a one-sentence remark in Abubakari and Appah 2024 that Kusaal has no stress, taken over from Hudu 2010 on Dagbani rather than from Kusaal data, while Musah 2010 describes the tone system without discussing stress at all.

Monosyllabic words retain stress only if they are of the ‟superheavy” form CVVC and/or precede pause; monosyllabic prefixes §6.1.2 are also unstressed. Bound and free words do not differ in stress behaviour; the term ‟clitic” will be reserved for left-bound words which partly or completely inhibit apocope of the preceding word §3.1. Prosodic enclitics §4.3 shift the stress of a preceding word to its last syllable. The language also differentiates between underlying high" [tones and downstepped highs]. p.137: "Kusaal has a three tone contrast - high, mid and low. Unlike Buli, however, there are instances of high tones which are realised as downstepped highs because of adjacent high tones." p.39: "Anonymous (nd: 9) notes that in these sequences of unlike vowels, the first parts usually take a stronger stress than the second."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kusaal has an empty rule. Musah 2010 adds that the language is a three-level-tone register language (mora TBU) and gives no word-stress placement; consistent with the catalog's empty placement, and with the supplementary on-disk statement (Abubakari & Appah 2024, GJL 13.2, p.10) that 'Stress marking is generally not a characteristic of Kusaal and Mabia languages'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kusaal is described as a register tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) plus downstepped high, with the mora as the tone-bearing unit (sec. 4.3, p.111). The thesis has no section on word stress and makes no statement about where stress falls or whether it exists; 'stress' appears only in general theoretical remarks (pp.19, 25, 141) and in one second-hand remark (p.39, citing an anonymous n.d. source) that within a vowel sequence (two moras in one syllable) the first vowel is more prominent than the second — a sequence-internal prominence, not a word-stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Musah 2010 describes the Ghanaian (Agole, Bawku/Zebilla) variety: data were recorded from twelve speakers at Bawku and Zebilla (abstract; p.145 summary). Niggli 2012 is about the Toende dialect of Burkina Faso and was not obtained. Kusaal is spoken in north-eastern Ghana, Burkina Faso and Togo.

new_statements.quote: [p.150, 5.5.2] L’accent d’intensité provoque un rehaussement du niveau mélodique du ton affectant la syllabe portant l’accent. L’accent d’intensité en kusaal est toujours sur l’avant-dernière syllabe du mot. [...] En kusaal, la place de l’accent d’intensité n’a aucune valeur distinctive. Cet accent marque automatiquement la première syllabe du mot phonologique sauf s’il s’agit d’un pronom ou d’une particule grammaticale. [p.11, 1.5.1] Accent : - Accent d’intensité sur la pénultième syllabe - épenthèse (insertion d’une voyelle) n’est pas comptée comme syllabe. [p.142] bà-kʋ́rʋ́k « vieux chien » [...] l’accent d’intensité est maintenant sur la deuxième = pénultième syllabe du mot prosodique, donc sur -'kʋ́rʋ́k
new_statements.translation: [p.150] The intensity (stress) accent raises the pitch register of the tone on the syllable that bears it. The stress accent in Kusaal is always on the second-to-last syllable of the word. [...] In Kusaal the position of the stress accent has no distinctive value. This accent automatically marks the first syllable of the phonological word unless it is a pronoun or a grammatical particle. [p.11] Accent: stress accent on the penultimate syllable; epenthesis (insertion of a vowel) is not counted as a syllable. [p.142] bà-kʋ́rʋ́k 'old dog' ... the stress accent is now on the second = penultimate syllable of the prosodic word, i.e. on -'kʋ́rʋ́k.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Kusaal with an empty rule and no existing statements; this work supplies an explicit placement (penultimate, non-contrastive, within a tone language). Note that other files already held by the project for kusa1250 from earlier passes (Musah 2010 MPhil on Ghanaian Kusaal; Abubakari & Appah 2024 p.10 'Stress marking is generally not a characteristic of Kusaal') treat Kusaal as tonal with no stress, so Niggli's Toende description differs from those Agole/Ghana-based sources in asserting a (non-phonemic) penultimate stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kusaal (Toende) is a tone language (lexical H and L, downstep, downdrift; sec. 5.1) that also has a non-contrastive dynamic stress ('accent d'intensité') fixed on the penultimate syllable of the phonological/prosodic word; epenthetic support vowels (written ɩ/ʋ, realised [ə]) do not count as syllables; the stressed syllable has a full, clearly articulated vowel and its tone is realised at a raised register (B+ / H+), unstressed medial vowels are short and centralised (3.7.4); pronouns and grammatical particles are not stressed; in noun+adjective prosodic words the stress is computed over the whole unit (bà-'kʋ́rʋ́k). The author states repeatedly (pp.11, 82, 87, 141, 150, 151) that stress is penultimate; one sentence on p.150 instead says it 'automatically marks the first syllable of the phonological word', which coincides with the penult for the typical disyllabic root+suffix word but is an internal inconsistency for trisyllables (his own p.142 example puts it on the penult, not the first syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: epenthetic vowels not counted as syllables (p.11, p.87); pronouns and grammatical particles do not take the accent (p.150); stress placement has no distinctive value (p.150); in noun+adjective compounds the accent moves to the penult of the whole prosodic word (p.142); for toneless-root nouns the accent supplies a default H (tonal class 3, p.141).
new_statements.identity_note: Niggli 2012 explicitly describes the Toende (tondé, western) variety of Kusaal as spoken in Burkina Faso (intro pp.7-9: 'le parler kusaal tondé dont traite notre description phonologique'); Agole (eastern, Ghana only) is named as the other dialect and is not described. The earlier on-disk sources for kusa1250 (Musah 2010; Abubakari & Appah 2024) are based mainly on Ghanaian Kusaal.

readall_conflicts: Within Niggli 2012 itself there is one inconsistent sentence: p.150 says both that the accent d'intensité 'est toujours sur l'avant-dernière syllabe du mot' and, a few lines later, that it 'marque automatiquement la première syllabe du mot phonologique'; every other statement in the book (pp.11, 82, 87, 141, 142, 151) and the worked trisyllabic example bà-'kʋ́rʋ́k (p.142, 'deuxième = pénultième syllabe') support penultimate, and the two coincide for the usual disyllabic word, so I read the source as fixed: penultimate syllable, non-contrastive. Across sources: the catalog record has no rule, so nothing is contradicted there; but the Ghana-based works already saved in this folder from earlier passes (Musah 2010, tone only, no stress section; Abubakari & Appah 2024, 'stress marking is generally not a characteristic of Kusaal') describe Kusaal as purely tonal without word stress, whereas Niggli (Toende dialect, Burkina Faso) posits a predictable penultimate intensity accent alongside H/L tone. This is a type difference (no-word-stress vs fixed non-phonemic stress) that may track dialect (Agole vs Toende) or analytic tradition.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Eddyshaw 2026 PDF we hold/txt at sec. 2.3 pp. 26-28, and the supporting prefix statement at sec. 6.1.2 p. 127; the p. 28 example explicitly places stress on the post-prefix root syllable, matching our 'morphological (root/stem-initial) stress' coding. (2) Deciding source is a current 423-pp reference grammar with an explicit stress section — the top Glottolog grammar for the language and the only work found that analyses Kusaal stress; no JIPA illustration, instrumental study or stress article exists in Crossref. (3) What we lack are the native-speaker descriptions (Musah 2018 grammar, Musah 2010 MPhil, Musah 2017 weight chapter) and Niggli 2012 for Toende; none is open-access from here. Two open items downloaded: Duah's 2020 review of Musah 2018 is silent on stress (tone-only phonology), and Abubakari & Appah 2024 p. 10 assert in one

sources.quote: 'Stress marking is generally not a characteristic of Kusaal and Mabia languages. For instance, Hudu (2010:19) asserts that "Dagbani and other Gur languages are not stress marking". Thus, this criterion cannot be applied to distinguish compounds from phrases in Kusaal.' — a one-sentence assertion (no data or analysis) by a native-speaker linguist that Kusaal has no stress; contradicts the existence of word stress rather than its location.
